content: Chronic cold urticaria, also known as cold hives, is a condition characterized by the development of hives or large, red, raised welts on the skin in response to cold stimuli. These welts are often itchy and may be accompanied by swelling, particularly in the hands and feet. The size of the hives can range from as small as a pencil eraser to as large as a quarter or even larger. When the condition persists for more than six weeks, it is classified as chronic. The course of the disease is unpredictable, and while it can last a lifetime, it most commonly affects individuals between the ages of 18 and 25. The primary symptoms of cold urticaria include red welts, wheals, or hives that can appear on the skin or mucous membranes. These hives may or may not be itchy and can last anywhere from a few minutes to several days, depending on the individual. A burning sensation is also commonly reported. In most cases, the exact cause is idiopathic, meaning it is unknown. However, in rare instances, cold urticaria may be associated with other underlying conditions, and further testing may be warranted if the presentation of the hives is atypical. Diagnosis of cold urticaria is typically performed by an allergist or other qualified healthcare provider using a cold stimulation test. During this test, a piece of ice is applied to the forearm for approximately 3 to 5 minutes. A positive result is indicated by the appearance of raised, red hives at the site of contact, which may take the shape of the ice or radiate outward from the contact area. For example, air-conditioned rooms and swimming pools may be too cold for individuals with this condition. Antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl), cetirizine (Zyrtec), or fexofenadine (Allegra), are commonly used to prevent or treat hives. In cases where there is a risk of a severe systemic reaction, individuals may need to carry an epinephrine auto-injector (e.g., EpiPen or Twinject) for emergency use. It is important to note that cold urticaria can sometimes cause reactions even in warm weather. For instance, sweat on the skin combined with a breeze can rapidly cool the skin and trigger hives. In such cases, drying the skin and covering up promptly can help control the reaction. Swimming poses a particular danger, as the combination of rapid heart rate and the onset of hives can lead to hypotension. Taking an antihistamine before swimming and conserving energy while acclimating to the water temperature may help reduce the risk of a severe reaction. Contrary to popular belief, immersing the affected area in hot water or moving to a warmer environment does not necessarily improve symptoms.
